ety: From Arabic زَعْتَر (zaʕtar), صَعْتَر (ṣaʕtar, “wild thyme; condiment made from this herb”), probably from Classical Syriac ܨܬܪܐ (ṣāṯrā), related to Hebrew צַתְרָה (ṣátrā).

s.def: A particular herb, similar in flavor to thyme or oregano, used in Middle Eastern cuisine (Origanum syriacum).
A Middle Eastern seasoning, having this herb or a mixture of herbs as the main ingredient, with sumac (or other tart-flavored equivalent) and sesame seeds.

ety: From Arabic زَبَانِيَة (zabāniya).

s.def: A group of angels in Islam who are tasked to torture the sinners in hell.

ety: From clipped forms of Zachariah and Zacharias + -y, from Hebrew זְכַרְיָה (Zəḵaryā, “Yahweh has remembered”) via Latin Zacharias and Koine Greek Ζαχαρίας (Zakharías). As an American city, named after the farmer Darel Zachary who sold the land for a local depot on the Illinois Central Railroad in the 1880s. Doublet of Zach, Zacharias, Zachariah, Zechariah, Zakariya, and Jakariya.

s.def: A male given name from Hebrew.
ex: Zachary Block chats with Carrie Brownstein and Fred Armisen about their new show, Portlandia, which airs on IFC, Fridays at 10:30.

s.def: A surname transferred from the given name.
A city in East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana, United States.
capital of Croatia
The capital and largest city of Croatia.
A county of Croatia.

ety: From Zagreb + -ian.

s.def: A native or inhabitant of Zagreb.

ety: Borrowed from French zaïre. Named after the Zaire River, another name for the Congo River.

s.def: The unit of currency of Zaire from 1967 to 1998.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Bantu *jade Kongo nzadi Kongo o Kongo nzere Kongo nzadi o nzereder. Portuguese Zairebor. French Zaïrebor. English Zaire Borrowed from French Zaïre, a truncation of Kongo nzadi o nzere (“river swallowing rivers”) which refers to the Congo river; adopted in accordance with the Authenticity Movement.

s.def: Former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo: a country in Central Africa; used from 1971–1997.
Synonym of Congo (major river in Central Africa)
A province of Angola, named after the river

ety: Borrowed from: * Persian زکات (zakât); * Turkish zekât, from Ottoman Turkish زكات (zekat); or * Urdu زَکَات (zakāt); all from Arabic زَكَاة (zakāh, “almsgiving, zakat; purification”), from زَكَوٰة (zakāh) (archaic), from Aramaic זכותא/ܙܟܘܬܐ (zākūṯā, “goodness, probity, uprightness; merit; victory”), from זכי (zəḵē, “to gain; to overcome, triumph over”).

s.def: Almsgiving, usually in the form of an annual tax on certain types of property which is then used for charitable purposes; the third of the five pillars of Islam.
ex: Services given by the Sayyids are supposed to be free, but they should receive the Zikat, or one tenth of the fruits of the earth.
In practice, the zakats seem to have varied a great deal with the context, the society, and local norms.

ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ζάκυνθος (Zákunthos). Doublet of Zante.

s.def: An island of Greece, on the Ionian Sea; the third-largest Ionian island.

ety: From Romanian Zalău.

s.def: A city in Sălaj County, Romania.

ety: From Zambezi. See Zambezi at Wikipedia.

s.def: A country in Southern Africa. Official name: Republic of Zambia. Formerly called Northern Rhodesia.

ety: From Zambia + -an.

s.def: A person from Zambia or of Zambian descent.

ety: Borrowed from Arabic زَمْزَم (zamzam).

s.def: An Islamic holy well in Mecca, supposed to have been miraculously generated by Allah when Abraham's infant son Ishmael was crying for water.

ety: Borrowed from Persian زَنْد (zand, “Zand (member of the Zand tribe)”), from Laki. Further etymology uncertain.

s.def: A member of the Zand tribe, a Laki-speaking Kurdish tribe of western Iran.
A member of the Zand dynasty, a ruling house of Iran (1751–1794) founded by Karim Khan Zand.

ety: Borrowed from German Zander, from a Slavic language, perhaps via Middle Low German sandāt. Pfeifer states that the first German attestation is East Central German czandas (in the Marienburger Treßlerbuch) circa 1400, which he derives from Pomeranian *sądač (compare Slovincian sãdzoc), from Proto-Slavic *sǫdakъ. Low Prussian forms include Zand, and other Slavic languages (e.g. Kashubian) have been considered as possible sources. Doublet of sandre.

s.def: A European freshwater fish in the family Percidae, closely related to the perch, Sander lucioperca.
Any fish of the genus Sander that live in freshwater.

ety: Quoting Clifford Edmund Bosworth, "the origin of the name Zangī is unclear; an obvious meaning would be 'black African' [from Persian زنگی (zangi)], possibly relating to a swarthy complexion, but this would be unusual for a Turk". Another theory considers the meaning "protector of cattle", compare 19th century Kirg. Zeñ-baba "protector spirit of cows".

s.def: ʿImād ad-Dīn Zangī (d. 541/1146), Turkmen founder of the Zangid dynasty which ruled northern Iraq and Syria between the 12th and 13th centuries.
Alternative form of zantewood.
A small, sweet, seedless black grape with an intense flavour when dried, from a cultivar of Vitis vinifera the grape vine.

ety: From Middle French zani, zanni, from Italian zanni (“a kind of masked clown character”), from Zanni, a Venetian form of Giovanni. Doublet of Zanni, John, and Giovanni.

s.def: Ludicrously or incongruously comical.
Unusual and awkward in a funny, comical manner; outlandish; clownish.
A fool or clown, especially one whose business on the stage is to imitate foolishly the actions of the principal clown.
To mimic foolishly.

ety: 1920s, American English, of imitative origin.

s.def: A sound made by a sudden release of electricity or some similar energy.
An electric shock.
ex: You might feel a little zap touching a metal doorknob when the air is dry.

s.def: A raucous public demonstration designed to embarrass a public figure or celebrity as a form of political activism.
ex: Black AIDS activists were caught in the middle of a nearly yearlong series of zaps.
When a zap at Brooklyn's Board of Education opened no dialogue on discrimination suffered by gay teachers, GAA targeted the BOE offices on April 13.

s.def: The act of heating something in a microwave oven.
ex: The guest immediately asked the bartender to give his drink a zap in the microwave oven behind him […]

s.def: To make a zap sound.
To use a remote control to repeatedly fast-forward or change channels on a television.
To strike (something or someone) with electricity or energy, as by shooting.
ex: They spent the whole movie zapping bad guys into oblivion.

s.def: To kill; to eliminate.
ex: Says a U. S. officer: "We zapped the enemy, now we intend to stick around. […]

s.def: To do away with something.
To enliven.

ety: From the historical region of the same name, Ukrainian Запорі́жжя (Zaporížžja, “place beyond the rapids”), from за (za, “beyond”) + поро́ги (poróhy, “rapids”), plural of порі́г (poríh, “river rapid, threshold”). Compare Russian Запоро́жье (Zaporóžʹje).

s.def: city in Ukraine
An industrial city, the administrative centre of Zaporizhzhia urban hromada, Zaporizhzhia Raion and Zaporizhzhia Oblast, in south-central Ukraine, on the River Dnipro.
A raion of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine. Administrative center: Zaporizhzhia.
An oblast in southeast Ukraine, also illicitly claimed by Russia. Administrative center: Zaporizhzhia.
A geographic region south-central Ukraine, “beyond the rapids” in the lower reaches of the Dnipro River, base of the Zaporozhian Cossacks.
Numerous villages in Ukraine:

ety: From French zaptieh, from Ottoman Turkish ضبطیه (zaptiye, “policeman”), from Arabic ضَبْطِيَّة (ḍabṭiyya, “policeman”).

s.def: A Turkish policeman.

ety: From Azerbaijani Zaqatala.

s.def: A city and district of Azerbaijan.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish Zaragoza, from Old Navarro-Aragonese Zaragoza, from Mozarabic, from Latin Caesaraugusta, named after Roman Emperor Augustus. Doublet of Caesaraugusta.

s.def: A city, the regional capital of Aragon, Spain.
A province of Aragon, Spain.
A barangay of Bugasong, Antique, Philippines.
A town in La Libertad department, El Salvador.
A barangay of Bolinao, Pangasinan, Philippines.
A municipality of Nueva Ecija, Philippines.
A barangay of Matalom, Leyte, Philippines.
A barangay of Surigao, Surigao del Norte, Philippines.
Saragossan; a native or inhabitant of the city of Zaragoza, Aragon, Spain.

ety: Likely borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ظَرْف (zarf), ultimately from Arabic ظَرْف (ẓarf). Also influenced by Classical Persian ظَرْف (zarf) and Hindustani (Hindi ज़र्फ़ (zarf) / Urdu ظَرْف (zarf)).

s.def: An ornamental container designed to hold a coffee cup or teacup and insulate it from the hand of the drinker.

ety: Inherited from Middle English sax (“knife”), from Old English seax, from Proto-West Germanic *sahs, from Proto-Germanic *sahsą. Doublet of sax.

s.def: A tool, similar to a hatchet, used to prepare slate for roofing.

ety: From Zazaki Zazaki.

s.def: The language spoken by the Zaza people of eastern Turkey.
ex: Zazaki has three sub-dialects: Northern, Central, and Southern Zazaki.

ety: From Middle English zele, from Old French zel, from Late Latin zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to search”). Related to jealous.

s.def: fervour or devotion
The fervour or tireless devotion for a person, cause, or ideal and determination in its furtherance; diligent enthusiasm; powerful interest.
ex: She extols the virtues of veganism with missionary zeal.
I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Zeal, the blind conductor of the will

s.def: A person who exhibits such fervour or tireless devotion.
A group of zebras.
ex: A zeal of zebras confuses predators. Each zebra has a different set of stripes.
Zebras can also be called a herd or a zeal.
These three were a part of a zeal of 30 zebras.

s.def: A light zomp.

ety: Borrowed from Danish Sjælland.

s.def: The largest island of Denmark.

ety: Initially only found as Middle English zelote, an epithet of Simon the Zealot, acquiring its current senses in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Middle English derives from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs, “emulator, zealous admirer, follower”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”), from ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”).

s.def: One who is zealous, one who is full of zeal for their own specific beliefs or objectives, usually in the negative sense of being too passionate; a fanatic.

A member of a radical, warlike, ardently patriotic group of Jews in Judea, particularly prominent in the first century, who advocated the violent overthrow of Roman rule and vigorously resisted the efforts of the Romans and their supporters to convert the Jews.
A member of an anti-aristocratic political group in Thessalonica from 1342 until 1350.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-los Proto-Indo-European *yéh₂los Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos)bor. Latin zēlus Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₃édosder.? Proto-Italic *-ŏ̄dsos? Old Latin -ōssus Latin -ōsus Latin zēlōsusder. Middle English zelose English zealous From Middle English zelose, from Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus + -ōsus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous…

s.def: Full of zeal; ardent, fervent; exhibiting enthusiasm or strong passion, particularly in matters of religion.
ex: Newt Gingrich […] left Congress in 1998, following GOP midterm-election losses that many blamed on his zealous pursuit of Bill Clinton's impeachment.

ety: First attested in 1600. Borrowed from Italian zebra, from Portuguese zebra, zebro (“zebra”), from Old Galician-Portuguese enzebro, ezebra, azebra (“wild ass”), from earlier cebrario (882), ezebrario (897), from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild horse”) (Pliny), from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”). While the word was traditionally pronounced with a long vowel in the first syllable in standard English, during the twentieth century a vowel shift occurred in regions of England,…

s.def: A biracial person, specifically one born to a Sub-Saharan African person and a white person.
Any of three species of subgenus Hippotigris: Equus grevyi, Equus quagga, or Equus zebra, all with black and white stripes and native to Africa.
ex: A group of zebras can be called a dazzle.

s.def: A referee.
An unlikely diagnosis, especially for symptoms probably caused by a common ailment.
Someone who has Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or hypermobility spectrum disorder
ex: EDS charities around the world use a zebra logo to promote the idea that sometimes it really is that ‘rare’ condition.

s.def: A zebra cichlid (Amatitlania nigrofasciata).
Any of various papilionid butterflies of the subgenus Paranticopsis of the genus Graphium, having black and white markings.
A zebra crossing.
ex: On his way home he'd picked up two economy-sized bags of tortilla chips, and had dropped both when a twat in a Lexus honked him on a zebra . . .

s.def: A fairy chess piece that is moved three squares in one direction and two at right angles to that direction in a single move, leaping over any intervening pieces.

ety: zebra + crossing From the similarity of the stripes to those of a zebra.

s.def: A pedestrian crossing featuring broad white stripes painted parallel to the street.
ex: 'Oh, that was easy,' says Man, and for an encore goes on to prove that black is white and gets himself killed on the next zebra crossing.
Do not ride across a pelican, puffin or zebra crossing. Dismount and wheel your cycle across.
The Abbey Road zebra crossing in north London — made famous after appearing on a Beatles album cover — has been given Grade II listed status.

s.def: A small Australasian weaverbird of the genus Taeniopygia that has markings similar to a zebra.

ety: The juvenile stage of this shark has stripes reminiscent of a zebra's.

s.def: A species of carpet shark, Stegostoma fasciatum, family Stegostomatidae, covered in black spots as adults.

ety: From zebra + fish.

s.def: A small striped fish of species Danio rerio, originally from India but now common as an aquarium fish and as a subject of genetic experiments.
ex: Use of the GAL4-UAS technique for targeted gene expression in the zebrafish.

s.def: A member of certain species of Percina (logperch).
Certain venomous lionfish, of genus Pterois.

ety: Borrowed from French zébu, probably from Tibetan མཛོ་པོ (mdzo po, “male bull–yak hybrid”), whence also zobo.

s.def: A domesticated ox native to Asia and Africa, having a large fleshy hump on its back and a dewlap (Bos taurus indicus or bos indicus).

ety: From Hebrew זְכַרְיָה (zəḵaryā, “the Lord has remembered”). Doublet of Zach, Zachary, Zachariah, Zacharias, Zakariya, and Jakariya.

s.def: A Hebrew prophet traditionally considered the author of the Book of Zechariah, the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets.
A Hebrew priest, the father of John the Baptist, considered a major prophet in Islam.
A male given name from Hebrew.
A king of Israel mentioned in the second book of Kings.
A book of the Old Testament and the Hebrew Tanakh.

ety: From Middle English zed, zedde, zede, from Old French zede, from Late Latin zeta, from Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta), from Hebrew ז (zayin) with influence from βῆτα (bêta), ἦτα (êta) and θῆτα (thêta). The letter had a rare usage in Old English, such as in bezt, where it represented "ts" (compare the German, Italian, and Finnish pronunciation of Z). For the sleep sense, see zzz. The zombie sense comes from the initial letter. Doublet of zeta. Cognate to Spanish zeta, German Zett, French zède, Italia…

s.def: The name of the Latin script letter Z/z.
ex: Zzz...With all those ʻzedsʼ I'll be sending you to sleep.

s.def: Something Z-shaped.
Sleep.
ex: I'm going to go get some zeds.

s.def: A zombie.
ex: A horde of zeds began to shuffle into the shopping mall.

s.def: To sleep or nap. (Compare zzz, catch some z's.)
ex: Zedding hogs. Sleep sippers and spitters. Look at 'em cooking in their own snoring heat. One nose after another.
I guess I must have zedded, for I find a police officer, the same one that nicked me, shaking me.

s.def: To zigzag; to move with sharp alternating turns.
ex: We were zedding hell-bells up the hill towards Cervione, with a bank of road metal and a precipice on our left...

ety: From Medieval Latin zedoārium, from Arabic جَدْوَار (jadwār), from Classical Persian ژدوار (žadwār).

s.def: Curcuma zedoaria, a perennial herb native to India and Indonesia.

ety: Likely an alteration of zed (which see for more), by analogy with other letters such as bee, dee, tee and vee. Fell out of usage in England by the 17th century, and made standard in the U.S. in American Dictionary of English Language by Noah Webster in 1828, though usage varied for decades afterwards.

s.def: The name of the Latin script letter Z/z.
ex: Thus first C checks to see if ex and wye are equal. The resulting value of 1 or 0 (true or false) then is compared to the value of zee.

s.def: Something Z-shaped. Found in compounds.
Sleep.
ex: Time to get some zees.

s.def: To sleep or nap. (Compare zzz, catch some z's.)
To zigzag; to move with sharp alternating turns.
Pronunciation spelling of the, representing primarily French or German accented English.

ety: From Dutch Zeeland.

s.def: A province of the Netherlands.
A village in North Brabant, Netherlands.
A city in Ottawa County, Michigan.
A city in McIntosh County, North Dakota.

ety: Unadapted borrowing from German Zeitgeist (literally “spirit of the age”).

s.def: The spirit of the age; the taste, outlook, and spirit characteristic of a period.
ex: [Robert] Heinlein’s gift was to catch the zeitgeist. “That’s what made him so successful, but it makes his work seem dated.”

ety: A transliteration of Ukrainian Зеле́нський (Zelénsʹkyj).

s.def: surname
A surname from Ukrainian.

ety: From New Latin (genus name) from Russian дзе́льква (dzélʹkva, “tree, wood”), from Georgian ძელქვა (ʒelkva), from Old Georgian ძელქვაჲ (ʒelkvay), from ძელი (ʒeli, “beam”) + ქვაჲ (kvay, “stone”).

s.def: A kind of tree in the elm family (genus Zelkova).

ety: Transliteration of Russian Земфи́ра (Zemfíra), name of the heroine in Pushkin's poem Цыга́ны (Cygány, “The Gypsies (1827)”). Possibly of Romani origin.

s.def: A transliteration of the Russian female given name Земфи́ра (Zemfíra).
Alternative spelling of zamindar.

ety: From Russian зе́мство (zémstvo), from земля́ (zemljá, “land, country”).

s.def: A Russian district or provincial council, or elective local-governmental administrative division, founded in 1864 by Tsar Alexander the Liberator.
ex: Two of Alexander III's counter-reforms, in 1890 and 1892, greatly increased the governors' powers over the zemstvos and municipal bodies.

ety: From Hindi ज़नाना (zanānā), Urdu زنانه (zanānah), from Classical Persian زنانه (zanāna, “womanly”), from زن (zan, “woman”). Related to Old English cwene (“woman”). More at quean.

s.def: Synonym of harem (“area of house or palace for high-caste women or wives of a wealthy man; the women thus kept; the system of segregating women in this way”).
ex: Yet inside the walls of the havelis and the lattice screens of the zenana, life goes on as it always did.
Out of the blue, the chief eunuch of the zenana appears.
‘You have more than enough to occupy you, I'm sure, with all your palaces and zenanas and budgerows.’

s.def: Synonym of sissy (“effeminate man”).
Synonym of bottom (“passive partner in male homosexual sex”), especially an effeminate one.
Synonym of trans woman.

ety: From Middle English cenyth, from Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”), from the fuller form سَمْت اَلرَّأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”). The -ni- for -m- is sometimes thought to be due to a misreading of the three strokes, which is plausible, though it could be a mere phonetic approximation.

s.def: The point in the sky vertically above a given position or observer; the point in the celestial sphere opposite the nadir.
ex: In the east a pillar of cloud reared from horizon to zenith, with a kind of arm outstretched like a threatening colossus.

s.def: The highest point in the sky reached by a celestial body.
ex: […] in the middle of the day, when the sun was in the zenith, the violence of the heat was too great to stir out […]

s.def: Highest point or state; peak.
ex: Winning the continental championship was the zenith of my career.
It was during those civil troubles […] this aspiring family reached the zenith.
"There for a while I enjoyed myself in the zenith of glory and pleasure."

ety: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).

s.def: Anything of fine, soft, or light quality, especially fabric.
A light wind from the west.
Any light refreshing wind; a gentle breeze.

A type of soft confectionery made by whipping fruit and berry purée (mostly apple purée) with sugar and egg whites with subsequent addition of a gelling agent like pectin, carrageenan, agar, or gelatine.
ex: For desserts there were “airy pie,” charlottes, mousses, kissel, plombir and “zephyrs.”
2 tablespoons beet juice (optional—include it if you’re nostalgic for pink zephyr)
The Russian zephyr and bird’s milk fillings rely on agar as a gelling agent

s.def: To blow or move like a zephyr, or light breeze.
ex: There was a time When the soft zephyring spring came joyfully, Like a young bride, with bloom upon her cheek—
There was a sudden scrambling and thumping overhead and hot exclamations zephyred down to them.
But there was a new afflation— / An aura zephyring round, / That care infected not: [...]

s.def: To blow or blow on gently like a zephyr; to cool or refresh with a gentle breeze.
Alternative letter-case form of Zeppelin.

ety: Borrowed from German Zeppelin. Named after Ferdinand von Zeppelin, whose surname derives from the German town name Zepelin. Doublet of cepelinas.

s.def: A type of large dirigible rigid airship of the early 20th century, built by the German Luftschiffbau Zeppelin and designed to carry passengers or bombs.
A rigid airship dirigible, not restricted to Germany nor the early 20th century.
The penis.

ety: Collectively borrowed from Early Modern Spanish zero, Middle French zero, and (their etymon) Old Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zēphirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing; cipher”), itself calqued from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnyá, “void; nothingness”). Doublet of cipher and chiffre. Cognate with Spanish cero and French zéro.

s.def: The cardinal number occurring before one and that denotes no quantity or amount at all, represented in Arabic numerals as 0.
ex: The conductor waited until the passenger count was zero.
A cheque for zero dollars and zero cents crashed the computers on division by zero.

s.def: The numeric symbol that represents the cardinal number zero.
ex: In unary and k-adic notation in general, zero is the empty string.
Write 0.0 to indicate a floating point number rather than the integer zero.
The zero sign in American Sign Language is considered rude in some cultures.

s.def: The value of a magnitude corresponding to the cardinal number zero.
ex: The electromagnetic field does not drop all of the way to zero before a reversal.

s.def: The point on a scale at which numbering or measurement originates.
ex: The temperature outside is ten degrees below zero.

s.def: The digit 0 in the decimal, binary, and all other base numbering systems.
ex: One million has six zeroes.

s.def: Nothing, or none.
ex: The shipment was lost, so they had zero in stock.
He knows zero about humour.
In the end, all of our hard work amounted to zero.

s.def: A person dismissed as unimportant.
ex: They rudely treated him like a zero.

s.def: A difference that is present at an abstract level, but not realized in the form, that is, superficially (on the surface).
A casual misspelling of Zero ("a fighter aircraft operated by Imperial Japan during World War II").
A setting of calibrated instruments such as a firearm, corresponding to a zero value.

syn: value of a function’s variables at zero

ety: From zero + -th (ordinal suffix).

s.def: In the initial position in a sequence whose elements are numbered starting at zero; the ordinal number corresponding to zero.
ex: The zeroth order polynomial approximation is constant.

s.def: Corresponding to a position preceding the first.
ex: A and C are in equilibrium following the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics.

ety: Borrowed from French zeste.

s.def: The outer skin of a citrus fruit, used as a flavouring or garnish.
ex: The orange zest gives the strong flavor in this dish.

s.def: General vibrance of flavour.
ex: I add zest to the meat by rubbing it with a spice mixture before grilling.
He rolled his own cigarettes from a sack of Bull Durham, spilling flakes into his beer, which no doubt gained in zest thereby.
Bashele’s dishes tasted as good as they had when I was a child. No one could give to the borscht such a sweet-and-sour zest as Bashele.

s.def: Enthusiasm; keen enjoyment; exciting and interesting; relish or gusto; a state of being zesty.
ex: Auntie Mame had a real zest for life.
The singers, male and female, wore blue jeans and long hair and had more zest than talent.

s.def: The woody, thick skin enclosing the kernel of a walnut.
ex: The green zest of walnuts was used by the women to shine their teeth and it also gave a beautiful rust colour to their lips.

s.def: State of being a flamboyant or effeminate homosexual.
To scrape the zest from a fruit.
To make more zesty.

ety: From the Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta). Doublet of zed.

s.def: The sixth letter of the modern Greek alphabet (Ζ, ζ) preceded by epsilon (Ε, ε) and followed by eta, (Η, η); or the seventh letter in the ancient Greek alphabet, in which it is preceded by digamma (Ϝ, ϝ)
A mathematical function, formally known as the Riemann zeta function.
ex: Zeta of 3 is irrational

s.def: function of the complex variable s that analytically continues the sum of the infinite series ∑ₙ₌₁ ᪲1/(nˢ) that converges when the real part of s is greater than 1.

ety: From Ancient Greek Ζεύς (Zeús). Doublet of Dyeus and Jove.

s.def: The supreme Deity and ruler of all Hellenic gods in Hellenism, husband to Hera.
A male given name.
A representative given name for a dog.
ex: 67 give zeus a bath Wash off whatever your dog rolled in over the weekend. It'll freshen up your house and you'll burn about 100 calories.

ety: Borrowed from Ukrainian Жито́мир (Žytómyr), after a legendary Slavic prince.

s.def: A city and raion of Ukraine, municipal and regional administrative centre of Zhytomyr Oblast.
An oblast in north-western Ukraine. Seat: Zhytomyr.
The large Indian civet (Viverra zibetha).

ety: Learned borrowing from Akkadian 𒅆𒂍𒉪 (ziqqurratum).

s.def: A temple tower of the ancient Mesopotamian valley, having the form of a terraced pyramid of successively receding stories
Any building with similar style or shape.
ex: He works in an old ziggurat of an office building.

ety: Attested from 1712. Borrowed from French zigzag (attested from 1662), possibly from a Germanic source via Walloon ziczac (although German Zickzack is attested only from 1703). Also, possibly from the shape of the letter Z, which appears twice in the word. Sense “drunk” from the zigzag movements of a drunk person.

s.def: A line or path that proceeds by sharp turns in alternating directions.
One of these sharp turns.
Moving in, or having a zigzag.
ex: His thoughts were fixed on one subject, and it was an effort to him to follow the zigzag remarks of his children—an effort which he did not make.
There, by dint of looking closely about me, I found a rough zig-zag descending path notched out: which I followed.
Right and left ranked the toothed and zigzag line of storm-torn heights, forming the series which culminated in the one beneath their feet.

s.def: Drunk.
To move or to twist in a zigzag manner.
ex: At the base this vent was dark, cool, and smelled of dry, musty dust. It zigzagged so that he could not see ahead more than a few yards at a time.

s.def: In a zigzag manner or pattern.

ety: Probably from Joe Zilch, a placeholder name (compare John Doe) used by Nunnally Johnson in his column in the Brooklyn Daily Eagle from 1923; in turn from Joe Zilch, an unseen character referenced in comedian Frank Tinney's stage routine. Compare the rare German surname Zilch.

s.def: (informal) nothing
A nobody: a person who is worthless in importance or character.
ex: President Henry P. Zilch. Chairman of the Board Charles D. Zilch. Treasurer Otto Zilch.
Bernarr MacZilch [for Bernarr Macfadden] and His Dynamic-Hooey System... The WEAKLING Who Became 'The World's Most Perfect Ass!'
Dinglegoofer, Mr. Zilch, indefinite nicknames.

s.def: Nothing, zero.
ex: Her search for decent home-made winter clothes came up with zilch, so she had to get imported stuff.
"If the homeless wind up with zilch," James retorted, veiling his indignation behind a malevolent smile, "it's because they deserve zilch."

ety: See -illion. An arbitrary coinage, appearing by 1916, on analogy of million, billion, trillion.

s.def: An unspecified large number (of).
ex: Low Man: 'Thanks again, Woody. I'll see you next time the world needs saving.' / Woody: 'Pfft, yeah. Only if we sell a zillion units!'
"We are certainly not blaming lower socioeconomic families for not talking to their kids - there are probably a zillion reasons why that happens."

A corrugated iron roof.
A zinc countertop.
To electroplate with zinc.
To coat with sunblock incorporating zinc oxide.

ety: Borrowed from Russian зинда́н (zindán), from Classical Persian زِنْدَان (zindān).

s.def: an improvised prison cell consisting of a hole in the ground covered with a metal grille or grate.

ety: Of onomatopoeic origin.

s.def: A short high-pitched humming sound, such as that made by a bullet or vibrating string.
ex: I heard a zing close to my head and looked up again. Five or six men were lined up on the deck above me with rifles shooting at the shark.

Zest or vitality.

To move very quickly, especially while making a high-pitched hum.
To address a witty insult or comeback to.
To make a zinging noise or sound.
A high pitched humming sound.

A male given name from Hebrew.
A female given name.
An association of the righteous.
A city and township in Lake County, Illinois, United States.
A national park of the United States, located in Utah.

A religion practiced throughout sub-Saharan Africa, most popular in Swaziland, consisting of a mixture of Protestantism and animism.
A Christian eschatological concept that links the migration of Jews to Palestine with apocalyptic events.

ety: Calque of Arabic الكِيَان الصِّهْيَوْنِيّ (al-kiyān aṣ-ṣihyawniyy). First use appears c. 1956. See citations page.

s.def: Israel, viewed by Palestinians and their supporters as an illegitimate regime ruled by Zionists.

ety: Onomatopoeic.

s.def: The high-pitched sound of a small object moving rapidly through air.
To move rapidly (in a specified direction or to a specified place) with a high-pitched sound.
ex: The bullet zipped through the air.

A zip fastener.

ex: I know zip about economics.

A zip file.
Synonym of zip zap zop
Synonym of convolution (“a type of mapping function”).
An ounce of marijuana.

A fastener used in clothing, bags, etc, comprised of two rows of teeth that are made to fit into each other by moving a slider along their length and opened again by moving the slider in the other direction.
A pressure-sensitive plastic closure.

ety: 1925, zip + -er. The trade name was registered in 1925 by B.F. Goodrich for “boots made of rubber and fabric,” claiming use of the name since June 1923. No longer a registered trademark.

s.def: A zip fastener.
ex: He got his T-shirt stuck in the zipper of his jacket.

s.def: A pressure-sensitive plastic closure, as on a Ziploc bag.
A leucine zipper.
A scar on a person's body.

s.def: An air patrol carried out at dawn or dusk.
A string of clothes pegs or clips attached to the body and then quickly pulled off.
A technique for arbitrarily traversing an aggregate data structure and updating its contents. See zipper (data structure).
A zipline.
To close a zipper.
ex: He zippered his sweater against the cold.

s.def: To put a zipper on an article.
ex: These fall jackets are zippered.

ety: From zip (“to move in haste; to make (something) move quickly”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘having the quality of’).

s.def: Energetic and lively.
ex: [T]he rising wind, cool and zippy from the far ice floes of Bering Straits— [...]
[John] Macy did not mention that the zippy, educational program for kids could not have been less like the slow-moving documentary for adults.

s.def: Quick, speedy.

ety: From German Zirkon, possibly via French zircon, formed in the 1780s from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn), borrowed from Middle Persian zlgwn' (/⁠zargōn⁠/). Doublet of jargoon.

s.def: A mineral occurring in tetragonal crystals, usually of a brown or grey colour and consisting of silica and zirconia.
A crystal of zircon, sometimes used as a false gemstone.
ex: A zircon princess, seemed to lost her senses

s.def: The oxide of zirconium, obtained as a white powder, and possessing both acid and basic properties. On account of its infusibility, and brilliant luminosity when incandescent, it is used as an ingredient of sticks for the Drummond light.

ety: From a New Latin coinage, from zircon. Doublet of jargonium.

s.def: A chemical element (symbol Zr) with an atomic number of 40, a strong, lustrous, grey-white transition metal mainly used as a refractory and opacifier.
ex: Do you like how I dance? / I've got zirconium pants / Consequential enough / To slip you into a trance

ety: Borrowed from German Zither, from Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “a kind of harp”). Doublet of cithara, cither, and guitar.

s.def: A musical instrument consisting of a flat sounding box with numerous strings placed on a horizontal surface, played with a plectrum or fingertips.
Related or similar instruments in other cultures, such as the Chinese guqin or Norwegian harpeleik; especially any chordophone without a neck, and with strings that pass over the body.
To play a zither.
ex: We wandered and fiddled and zithered and tambourined through France till the chills and rains of autumn rendered our vagabondage less merry.

s.def: To make a sound similar to that made by a zither; to move while making such a sound.
ex: The olives seemed weighed down under the weight of their fruit, smooth drops of green jade among which the choirs of cicadas zithered.
‘Look at that!’ she shouted, already backing up the Jeep, its tyres zithering on the crusty surface.
The other men opened fire with pistols, slugs zithering past him with a dull whine.

ety: Borrowed from Greek ζιβανία (zivanía).

s.def: A traditional Cypriot alcoholic beverage made from grape pomace and wine.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰólh₃-tom Proto-Balto-Slavic *źálˀtader. Proto-Slavic *zoltъ Old Polish złoty Polish złotybor. English zloty Borrowed from Polish złoty.

ety: From Middle English zodiak (late 14th century), from Old French zodiaque, from Latin zōdiacus, from Ancient Greek ζῳδιακός [κύκλος] (zōidiakós [kúklos], “[circle] of little animals”), from ζῴδιον (zōídion), the diminutive of ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).

s.def: The belt-like region of the celestial sphere, approximately eight degrees north and south of the ecliptic, which includes the apparent path of the sun, moon, and visible planets.
The twelve equal divisions of the zodiacal region into signs or houses, each named for a prominent constellation in the region.
The ecliptic: the belt-like region of the celestial sphere corresponding to the apparent path of the sun over the course of a year.
Any of various astrological systems considered similar to the above.
ex: Discussing both Chinese and Western zodiacs might be a prewriting activity.
So the Dendera Zodiac seems to be a complete copy of the Mesopotamian zodiac.

s.def: A circle decorated with the signs of the zodiac.
A inflatable boat.
Any of the twelve star signs corresponding to the constellations which make up the zodiac.
ex: What’s your zodiac sign?

ety: First attested in the 18th century. Partially through Louisiana Creole zombi (“zombie; ghost”), Haitian Creole zonbi (“zombie”), and French zombi (“zombie”). Ultimately from a Bantu language. Compare Kongo nzambi (“god”), zumbi (“fetish”), and Kimbundu nzumbi (“ghost”) (see Portuguese zumbi, Sranan Tongo dyumbi), and Caribbean folklore's jumbie (“a spirit or demon”).

s.def: A person, usually undead, animated by unnatural forces (such as magic), with no soul or will of his or her own, typically being slow, obedient, and harmless unless directed to be harmful.
ex: Betsy Connell: I don't know about zombies, doctor. Just what is a zombie? / Dr. Maxwell: A ghost. A living dead. It's also a drink.
The zombies were having fun The party had just begun The guests included Wolf-Man, Dracula, and his son.

s.def: A dead person, reanimated through some fictional agency as a fungus, virus, or the like, that has an insatiable desire to eat living humans, typically depicted as aggressive, fast moving, and infectious.
ex: Ashley: Dad passed on a few years back. He's probably still watching, though. Shepard: He's not a zombie, is he?

s.def: An apathetic or slow-witted person.
A human being in a state of extreme mental exhaustion.
ex: After working for 18 hours on the computer, I was a zombie.

s.def: Someone or something that should be dead but is not.
An information worker who has signed a nondisclosure agreement.
A process or task which has terminated but has not been removed from the list of processes, typically because it has an unresponsive parent process.
A computer affected by malware which causes it to do whatever the attacker wants it to do without the user's knowledge.
A cocktail of rum and fruit juices.
ex: Betsy Connell: I don't know about zombies, doctor. Just what is a zombie? / Dr. Maxwell: A ghost. A living dead. It's also a drink.
She takes the taxi to the good hotel / Bon marché as far as she can tell / She drinks the zombie from the cocoa shell
The maitre d’ introduced us and I had a zombie with him. Those zombies are wicked. […] I watched Mario and drank zombies out of a thermos.

s.def: A conscripted member of the Canadian military during World War II who was assigned to home defence rather than to combat in Europe.

ety: From zombie + -fy.

s.def: To turn into a zombie (a member of the living dead or undead).
ex: She managed to flee the sorcerer who had attempted to zombify her and enjoyed relative prosperity in Jamaica.

s.def: To take control of (a computer) in order to use it covertly and illicitly.
ex: These trojans can zombify your machine.

s.def: To deprive of authenticity or vitality; to render someone brainless or unthinking.
ex: Zombified by the lies they said, we’ve become the walking dead.

ety: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”). Doublet of zona.

s.def: Each of the five regions of the earth's surface into which it was divided by climatic differences, namely the torrid zone (between the tropics), two temperate zones (between the tropics and the polar circles), and two frigid zones (within the polar circles).
Any given region or area of the world.
A given area distinguished on the basis of a particular characteristic, use, restriction, etc.
ex: There is a no-smoking zone that extends 25 feet outside of each entrance.
The white zone is for loading and unloading only.
Files in the Internet zone are blocked by default, as a security measure.

s.def: A restricted category or virtual place.

s.def: A semicircular area in front of each goal.

s.def: A defensive scheme where defenders guard a particular area of the court or field, as opposed to a particular opposing player.
That collection of a domain's DNS resource records, the domain and its subdomains, that are not delegated to another authority.
A belt or girdle.

ety: Calque of Russian зо́на ближа́йшего разви́тия (zóna bližájševo razvítija), coined by Soviet psychologist and social constructivist Lev Vygotsky.

A province of Turkey, on the Black Sea coast.

ety: Clipping of zoological garden or zoological park, now the usual form. See zoology. * Sense 5 is a clipping of zoophile or zoophilia.

s.def: A park where live animals are exhibited.
ex: The London Zoo was built in 1828.

s.def: Any place that is wild, crowded, or chaotic.
ex: The shopping center was a zoo the week before Christmas.

s.def: A large and varied collection of something.
ex: From this point on, an entire zoo of possibilities arose: strange stars, different families of neutron stars, hybrid stars, etc.

s.def: The jungle.

like feeding time at the zoo

ex: Meronym: ethology

s.def: A treatise on this science.

ety: Uncertain. The verb was first attested c. 1892, as a noun in 1918 and as an interjection in 1942. ex: the zoom of traffic

ex: What's the zoom like on your camera?

To move fast with a humming noise.

s.def: To zoom climb.

ety: From zoo- + (itself from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”)) + Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, “disease”) (compare also nosology); the surface analysis is almost, although not quite, zoo- + -osis; compare also anthroponosis.

relating to or characteristic of Zoroastrianism.
of, by or pertaining to Zoroastrianism.

ety: Borrowed from Latin zōstēr (“shingles”), from Ancient Greek ζωστήρ (zōstḗr, “girdle”).

s.def: An ancient Greek waist-belt for men.
The disease called herpes zoster (from the typically beltlike pattern of its rash); shingles.

ety: Minced form of God's wounds, with reference to the wounds from Christ's crucifixion. Compare strewth, blimey, gadzooks, 'sblood, crikey.

s.def: Expressing anger, surprise, assertion etc.
ex: 'Zounds, a dog, a rat, a mouse, a cat, to scratch a man to death!
Bounds, mounds, lounds, founds, kounds, downds, rounds, pounds, zounds! — hounds — ha! hounds — I have it.
"Zounds!" he exclaimed. "What the dickens is that?"

ety: Borrowed from Italian zucchetto, ultimately a diminutive of zucca (“gourd, squash”), due to the shape. Compare zucchini.

s.def: A small skullcap worn by Roman Catholic clergy (the Pope's is white, a cardinal's red, a bishop's purple, and a priest's black), Anglican clergy, and Syriac or Malankara Orthodox clergy

ety: Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino, diminutive of zucca (“squash”). Ultimately related to courgette through the original Latin cucurbita. Compare Sicilian cucuzza.

s.def: A courgette; a variety of squash, Cucurbita pepo, which bears edible fruit.
The edible fruit of this variety of squash.
plural of zucchino
Alternative letter-case form of Zulu from the NATO/ICAO Phonetic Alphabet.

ety: Etymology tree Zulu umu- Proto-Bantu *ʊ́- Zulu ú- Proto-Bantu *ìgʊ̀dʊ̀ Zulu ī́zulu Zulu úZulu Zulu uḿZuluder. English Zulu Derived from Zulu uḿZulu.

s.def: Pertaining to the Zulu people, culture, or language.
ex: If he puts in a Zulu word, that means there are Zulu people in the Belt.

ety: Etymology tree Celticder. Latin Turicumbor. Old High German Zurih German Zürichbor. English Zurich Borrowed from German Zürich.

s.def: The capital city of Zurich canton, Switzerland, on Lake Zurich.
ex: The Zurich group has shared a preliminary writeup of its findings.

s.def: canton
A canton of Switzerland.

ety: From Turkish zurna, from Ottoman Turkish زورنا (zurna), from Classical Persian سرنا (surnā); see there for more. Cognate with English horn, Latin cornu (“horn”).

s.def: A double-reed outdoor wind instrument, usually accompanied by a davul (bass drum) in Anatolian folk music.

ety: From German Zwieback, from zwie- (“twi-, two-”) + backen (“to bake”) (i.e. “twice-baked”), a calque of Italian biscotto (but not to be confused with it).

s.def: A form of rusk, usually sweetened bread enriched with eggs that is baked and then sliced and toasted until dry and crisp; considered easy to digest and therefore given to the ill and used as a teething food for toddlers.
ex: Ogden Nash, Adventures Of Isabel She nibbled the zwieback that she always fed off, And when it was gone, she cut the giant's head off.

ety: From Ancient Greek ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”).

s.def: union
pair

ety: From zygo- + -dactyl.

s.def: Having two toes pointing forward, and two pointing backward; zygodactylous.
Any bird with toes of this kind, such as the parrot.

ety: From Ancient Greek ζύγωμα (zúgōma), from ζυγόν (zugón, “yoke”), a connector for joining animals.

s.def: The cheekbone.

ety: From zygoma + -tic. Doublet of zygomaticus.

s.def: Of, relating to, or located in the area of the zygomatic bone or zygomatic arch.
ex: They show (1) the left orbit and zygomatic arch of President Kennedy magnified from Zapruder frame 230

s.def: Ellipsis of zygomatic bone.

ety: From zygo- + -osis.

s.def: The union of gametes to form a zygote; conjugation.
ex: Near-synonym: zygogenesis

ety: From zygo- + spore.

s.def: A zygosperm.
A spore formed by the union of several zoospores.

ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ζῠγωτός (zŭgōtós, “yoked”) + English -ote (suffix meaning ‘having [the thing to which it is attached]’). Ζῠγωτός (Zŭgōtós) is derived from ζῠγόω (zŭgóō, “to join or yoke together”) + -τός (-tós, suffix forming adjectives of possibility); and ζῠγόω (zŭgóō) from ζῠγόν (zŭgón, “yoke for joining animals; anything which joins two things together”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to tie together, join, yoke”)) + -όω (-óō, suffix forming causative or…

s.def: A eukaryotic cell formed from the fusion of two gametes (“reproductive cells”) during a fertilization process.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs Proto-Indo-European *yúHs-meh₂ Ancient Greek ζύμη (zúmē)bor. English zyme Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven”).

s.def: A ferment.
Synonym of microzyme.

ety: From zymo- (prefix meaning ‘fermentation’) + -logy (suffix denoting the study of a particular subject).

s.def: The chemistry of fermentation with yeasts, especially the science involved in beermaking and winemaking; zymurgy.
A treatise on the use of fermentation to produce liquors.

ety: From zymo- + -lysis.

s.def: The action of enzymes in breaking down organic substances during fermentation

ety: From zym- + -osis.

s.def: A fermentation
A process by which an infectious disease is believed to be developed, seen as similar to the process of fermentation, and caused by so-called microzymes, also known as zymes.
ex: zymosis of a healthy organism

s.def: A zymotic disease.

ety: From Ancient Greek ζυμωτικός (zumōtikós, “causing fermentation”), from ζυμοῦν (zumoûn).

s.def: Of or causing fermentation.
Infectious, contagious, of diseases originally regarded as being caused by a process similar to fermentation.
ex: Farr concluded that overcrowding was the main determinant of high mortality from what (following Liebig) he style ‘zymotic diseases’.

ety: From zym- (prefix meaning ‘fermentation’) + -urgy (suffix denoting a technique for working with something), modelled after metallurgy.

s.def: Synonym of zymology (“the chemistry of fermentation with yeasts, especially the science involved in beermaking and winemaking”).
ex: The natural languages, however, cover every subject from aardvarks to zymurgies.

s.def: The practice of using fermentation to produce alcoholic beverages.
ex: Of Zymurgy I little know, / Perhaps because I little knead, / And can but make a sorry show / In singing liaisons of feed, / Flour, fodder,— […]

ety: From Latin zȳthum, from Ancient Greek ζῦθος (zûthos).

s.def: An unfermented kind of Egyptian malt beer.

ety: Conventionalized sound of snoring.

s.def: A snoring sound, implying that somebody is asleep.
To sleep or snore.
ex: He lay back on his pillow, made a faint zzzing sound that ceased, and presently and quite quietly he died — greatly comforted by my assurance.
